objectives: Evaluate compound propositions and build truth tables from memory.

cards.front: How many rows in a truth table with 4 variables?
cards.back: 2^4 = 16 rows — one per assignment.

cards.front: State De Morgan's law for AND.
cards.back: NOT (p AND q) = (NOT p) OR (NOT q).

cards.front: State De Morgan's law for OR.
cards.back: NOT (p OR q) = (NOT p) AND (NOT q).

cards.front: Which are equivalent to p → q: converse, contrapositive, inverse?
cards.back: Only the contrapositive (¬q → ¬p). Converse and inverse are not equivalent.

cards.front: Name the four standard proof methods.
cards.back: Direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction.

cards.front: When is proof by contradiction the right tool?
cards.back: When assuming the negation gives you something concrete to push to an absurdity (e.g., irrationality proofs).

cards.front: What does the induction step require?
cards.back: Base case P(n0) proven, then P(k) → P(k+1) for arbitrary k ≥ n0.

cards.front: Why verify logic by brute force in Python?
cards.back: Exhaustive enumeration settles every row — the machine checks what your hand might miss.

quiz.q: A truth table for (p ∧ q) → r has how many rows?
quiz.explain: Three variables → 2^3 = 8 rows.

quiz.q: Which is logically equivalent to 'If the server is patched, then it is compliant'?
choices: If the server is compliant, then it is patched
If the server is not compliant, then it is not patched
If the server is not patched, then it is not compliant
quiz.explain: The contrapositive (¬q → ¬p) is the only equivalent restatement.

quiz.q: De Morgan's law: ¬(p ∨ q) equals…
quiz.explain: NOT (p OR q) = (NOT p) AND (NOT q).

quiz.q: To prove 'for all n, P(n)' by induction you must show…
quiz.explain: Base case plus the inductive step — both, or the proof is incomplete.

quiz.q: Proof by contradiction starts by assuming…
quiz.explain: Assume ¬P, derive an absurdity, conclude P.

quiz.q: Which study habit does IL-20 demand most?
choices: Working problems with pencil and paper before checking solutions
quiz.explain: Mathematics is learned by doing — the hand teaches what the eye skims.

items.prompt: Write the truth table for p → q and mark the one false row.
items.answer: False only when p is true and q is false; true on the other three rows.
items.explain: Implication is false exactly when the premise holds and the conclusion fails.

items.prompt: Verify De Morgan's AND law on all 4 rows.
items.answer: ¬(p∧q) and (¬p∨¬q) agree on all four assignments: T,T→F; T,F→T; F,T→T; F,F→T.
items.explain: Row-by-row agreement is the proof.

items.prompt: Give the contrapositive of: 'If n² is even, then n is even.'
items.answer: If n is odd, then n² is odd.
items.explain: Contrapositive: negate both sides and swap.

items.prompt: State the induction hypothesis for proving 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2.
items.answer: Assume the formula holds for k; prove it for k+1.
items.explain: The hypothesis is the bridge from k to k+1.

items.prompt: Can you solve a 2x2 linear system by elimination without looking anything up?
items.answer: Honest self-assessment; if not, review elimination before M05.
items.explain: IL-20's linear algebra modules assume this is fluent.

items.answer: Honest self-assessment; M04 builds on these from zero but rewards familiarity.

handsOnLab.title: Brute-force logic verifier in Python
handsOnLab.brief: Write a Python script that enumerates all truth assignments for two and three variables, verifies De Morgan's laws and the contrapositive equivalence on every row, and prints a formatted truth table. The machine settles every row; your job is to make the machine do it correctly.

modules.title: Sets & Propositional Logic
modules.summary: Welcome to IL-20, Mathematics for Engineers & Scientists. I'm your instructor for this course, and this is Module 1: Sets & Propositional Logic. Over the next few lessons we're going to build the logical language every proof in this course is written in — sets and their operations, propositions and connectives, truth tables, and quantifiers. By the end you'll read and write statements like ∃x ∀y P(x,y) without flinching, and you'll never confuse necessary with sufficient again.
objectives: Use set notation and the core operations: union, intersection, difference, complement
Evaluate compound propositions with truth tables
Translate statements into quantifier notation
Distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
Project brief
notes.body: Specify the access rules for a small internal tool as propositions. Define two sets — users and resources — and write the authorization rule as a compound proposition over membership statements (e.g., `admin ∨ (owner ∧ ¬suspended)`). Build its truth table, then use De Morgan's laws to write the exact negation of your rule, and prove the two tables are complements. Deliverable: the rule, both truth tables, and one paragraph arguing whether your rule makes access the necessary or the sufficient condition — and which direction is safer when the rule is wrong.

modules.title: Proof Methods
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 2: Proof Methods. I'm your instructor, and this is the module where mathematics becomes a skill instead of a spectator sport. We're going to drill the four moves that prove theorems, verify algorithms, and certify loop invariants — direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction, and mathematical induction. By the end you'll look at a claim like ‘the sum of the first n odd numbers is n²’ and reach for the right tool without hesitation.
objectives: Prove a statement directly from definitions
Use contrapositive and contradiction correctly
Carry out an induction proof including the base case and inductive step
Recognize where induction applies to algorithms and recurrences

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
Project brief
notes.body: Prove a loop invariant for a small algorithm of your choice — for example, binary search's ‘if the target is present, it lies in [lo, hi]’, or insertion sort's ‘the prefix is sorted’. Write the base case (invariant holds before the first iteration), the inductive step (each iteration preserves it), and the conclusion (the invariant plus the exit condition implies correctness). Deliverable: the invariant, the two proofs, and one paragraph naming the exact line where a plausible bug would break the step — induction finds bugs by forcing you to name what each iteration preserves.

modules.summary: Welcome to Module 13: Statistics. I'm your instructor. Probability told you how uncertainty behaves; statistics tells you how to learn from data anyway: sampling, the Central Limit Theorem, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing. The two sentences that matter most: a 95% confidence interval describes the procedure, not the parameter — and a p-value is P(data | H₀), never P(H₀ | data). Get those right and you'll avoid the two most expensive misreadings in applied science.

Construct and interpret a confidence interval
Run a hypothesis test and interpret the p-value correctly

modules.title: Linear Systems & Optimization
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 16: Linear Systems & Optimization — the final module. I'm your instructor, and we close the course where engineering lives: solving Ax=b at scale and minimizing objectives. Gaussian elimination, LU factorization, least squares, and gradient descent — the last one being the engine of neural-network training, built from the chain rule you learned in Module 8 and the gradients from Module 11. By the end you'll solve systems like a library does and tune a learning rate without superstition.
objectives: Solve Ax=b by Gaussian elimination with back substitution
Formulate and solve a least-squares problem
Run gradient descent on a convex objective
Explain the normal equations and when to avoid them

notes.body: Fit a least-squares line to a small dataset (six (x,y) points of your choosing, roughly linear with noise) twice: once via the normal equations AᵛAx = Aᵛb, once via QR factorization. Compare the solutions and explain — via the condition-number squaring from the Concepts section — why they can differ on ill-conditioned data. Then run five gradient-descent steps by hand on f(x) = x²+4x+6 with α = 0.1 from x=5 and report the trajectory toward the true minimum at x=−2. Deliverable: both fits, the comparison paragraph, and the descent trajectory.

import random
import math

N = 200000
inside = 0

    x = random.random()

scenarios.title: Choosing a Root-Finding Method
scenarios.context: You must find where a sensor calibration curve f(x) crosses zero on [0, 5]. f is smooth, you can evaluate f and f' cheaply, and you know f(0) < 0 < f(5). A wrong answer ships bad calibrations.

steps.prompt: First decision: which method do you start with?

options.text: Bisection on [0,5] — guaranteed, then polish with Newton
options.why: The sign change guarantees a root exists; bisection brackets it safely, and Newton's method then converges quadratically near the root.
Newton's method has no global guarantee — a poor start can diverge or cycle. Bracket first.

options.text: Sample f at 1000 points and pick the smallest |f|
options.why: Grid sampling gives no error bound and can miss narrow crossings entirely.

steps.prompt: After bisection narrows the bracket to width 1e-3, the root is needed to 1e-9. Next step?

options.text: Switch to Newton's method inside the bracket
options.why: Quadratic convergence near a simple root reaches 1e-9 in a few iterations from a 1e-3 bracket.
Works but wasteful: bisection needs ~10 more steps per decimal digit; Newton does it in 2-3.
The requirement is 1e-9; shipping 1e-3 violates the spec.

scenarios.title: Which Statistical Test?
scenarios.context: Two web-page variants ran for a week: A converted 120/2000 visitors, B converted 150/2000. The team wants to know if B is really better or the gap is noise.

steps.prompt: What is the right first analysis?

options.text: Two-proportion z-test (or chi-square) for the difference
options.why: Two independent binomial proportions — the z-test for difference in proportions (equivalently chi-square) is the standard tool.

options.text: A t-test on the raw conversion counts
options.why: A t-test assumes roughly normal continuous data; these are binary outcomes aggregated as proportions.
The 30-visitor gap may be noise; without a test you cannot separate signal from sampling variation.

steps.prompt: The test gives p = 0.04. The correct conclusion?

options.text: Reject the null at 5%: evidence B differs from A, and the direction favors B
options.why: p < 0.05 with the observed direction favoring B supports a real difference — while reporting the effect size (1.5 percentage points) and CI.

options.text: There is a 96% chance B is better
options.why: A p-value is not the probability the alternative is true — it is P(data this extreme | null).

options.text: p = 0.04 is too close to 0.05 to act on
options.why: The pre-chosen alpha was 0.05; moving the goalpost after seeing the data invalidates the test.

scenarios.title: Formulating an Optimization
scenarios.context: A warehouse must assign delivery routes minimizing total fuel cost. Costs are linear in distance, each truck has a capacity limit, every stop must be visited exactly once. 200 stops, 12 trucks.

steps.prompt: How do you frame this problem?

options.text: Mixed-integer linear program (or VRP heuristic) — discrete routing with capacity constraints
options.why: Visit-once + capacity + linear costs is a vehicle-routing / integer-programming structure; gradient descent cannot handle the discrete assignment.

options.text: Gradient descent on a smooth relaxation of the routes
options.why: Routes are discrete permutations; a smooth relaxation loses the visit-once structure and rounds badly.

options.text: Least squares fit of cost vs distance
options.why: That estimates a cost model — it does not choose routes.

steps.prompt: The MILP solver stalls on 200 stops. What now?

options.text: Use a construction + local-search heuristic (e.g., savings algorithm + 2-opt) and bound the gap
options.why: VRP is NP-hard; industry practice is good heuristics with lower bounds to certify solution quality.

options.text: Reduce to 12 stops so the solver finishes
options.why: Solving a different, smaller problem does not serve the 200 real stops.
The problem is combinatorial, not smooth — more gradient steps solve nothing.

faq.a: Read actively: cover the proof, attempt it, then compare. Keep a personal lemma library. Proofs are read like code — execute them by hand on examples.

faq.a: Yes — gradients, Jacobians, and constrained optimization (Lagrange) are the language of training. IL-12's backprop module assumes this.

faq.q: What's the single most useful topic for programmers?
faq.a: Discrete math (logic, combinatorics, graphs, induction) — it's the mathematics of computation itself. Linear algebra is second, for ML/graphics.

branchingScenarios.title: Find the flaw: the broken induction

claim.text: A classmate 'proves' by induction that all horses are the same color. Base case n=1: trivially true. Inductive step: assume any k horses share a color; for k+1 horses, remove one horse — the remaining k share a color by hypothesis — then put it back and remove a different one. All k+1 share a color. Where is the flaw?

choices.label: The inductive step fails at k=1: the two k-sets don't overlap
choices.feedback: Correct. For k=1, the two 1-horse subsets are disjoint — there is no overlapping horse to transfer the color. The step k→k+1 needs the intersection of the two k-sets to be nonempty, which fails exactly at the base. A proof is a machine: one broken gear stops it.

choices.label: The base case is wrong
choices.feedback: The base case is fine — one horse trivially has 'one color'. The break is in the step. Look at k=1.

choices.label: Induction doesn't apply to colors
choices.feedback: Induction applies to any well-defined property of natural numbers. The flaw is structural, not topical.

problem.text: Minimize f(x,y) = x² + 2y² subject to x + y = 10, with x,y ≥ 0. Which method fits?

choices.label: Lagrange multipliers — equality constraint, smooth objective
